## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll understand what workflow automation is, how the trigger → action model works, and how AI adds a reasoning layer in the middle. You'll also have a clear map of the tools covered in Part 10.

## Automation = Connecting Apps So They Talk

Workflow automation means wiring two or more apps together so that when something happens in one, something else happens automatically in another — without you doing it manually.

You already understand this concept intuitively:
- You get a new email → you copy the data into a spreadsheet
- A customer fills out a form → you send them a welcome message
- You push code to GitHub → someone on Slack gets a notification

Right now, a human is doing the connecting step. Automation removes that human step and makes it instant, reliable, and free.

The core model is always the same: **Trigger → Action**.

A **trigger** is the event that starts the workflow. Something happens — an email arrives, a form is submitted, a schedule fires at 9am.

An **action** is what happens in response. Send a message, add a row to a spreadsheet, create a task, call an API.

Multi-step workflows look like: Trigger → Action 1 → Action 2 → Action 3.

Here are simple examples:
- New row in Google Sheets → Send email via Gmail
- GitHub issue opened → Create Notion task
- Form submitted → Add to Airtable + Send Slack notification
- Calendar event starts → Send SMS reminder
**The one-sentence version:** Automation means "every time X happens, do Y automatically" — and you only set it up once.

## Where AI Fits In

Traditional automation is rule-based: IF new email FROM boss@company.com, THEN forward to assistant@company.com. The rules are rigid — if the email is from boss@company.com but arrives on a different domain, the rule breaks.

AI adds a **reasoning step** in the middle:

**Trigger → AI processes → Action**

Now instead of rigid rules, you can have flexible intelligence:
- New email arrives → Claude reads it and decides if it needs action → Creates a task only if it does
- RSS article published → Claude summarizes it into 2 sentences → Posts summary to Slack
- GitHub issue opened → Claude drafts a response based on similar past issues → Creates a draft reply

The AI step can classify, summarize, extract, decide, write, or transform — anything you'd ask a smart assistant to do.

This is why the automation tools in this part have an "AI node" or "AI action": they're designed specifically for this trigger → AI → action pattern.

## The Tools Landscape

Part 10 covers four tools at different points on the complexity spectrum:

**n8n** (lesson 10-2) — Open-source, can be self-hosted or run in the cloud via n8n.io. The most powerful free option. Has a native Claude/AI node. Slightly more technical than Zapier but far more flexible and free.

**Zapier** (lesson 10-3) — The most polished no-code option. Easiest setup. The AI action step requires a paid plan. Best for people who want simple workflows without any technical friction.

**Make (formerly Integromat)** (lesson 10-4) — Visual, cloud-based, module-oriented. Free tier is generous. No official Claude module, but the HTTP module lets you call the Anthropic API directly. Good middle ground between Zapier and n8n.

**GitHub Actions** (lesson 10-6) — Code-based CI/CD automation that runs on git events. Less "app connector" and more "developer pipeline." AI helps by generating the YAML configuration files you need.

The right tool depends on your situation:
- Want free + powerful → n8n
- Want easiest setup → Zapier (free tier for non-AI workflows)
- Want visual + flexible → Make
- Working with code/git → GitHub Actions
**You don't need to use all of them.** The goal of Part 10 is to understand what's possible with each tool. Most people pick one or two that fit their life and use only those.

sections.title: Automation Audit
sections.content:
Before touching any tools, do this audit. Open a notes file (in VS Code, Notepad, or a Google Doc) and write down **5 tasks you do repeatedly** that follow a pattern.

Use this format for each:
```
Trigger: [something that happens]
What I currently do: [the manual step]
Desired action: [what should happen automatically]
```

Examples to get you thinking:
- "Every time I get a receipt email, I manually log it in a spreadsheet"
- "Every morning I check 3 news sites to see what happened overnight"
- "Every time I finish a GitHub task, I update a Notion board"
- "Every week I summarize what I worked on for a report"

These 5 tasks are your automation targets. You'll build at least one of them in lessons 10-2 through 10-4.

**You've completed lesson 10-1.** You now understand the trigger → action model, how AI slots into the middle, and which tool fits which situation. The next three lessons build real, working automations using n8n, Zapier, and Make.
